mission.apollo-lunar.here: The same Saturn V to the kilogram, with the command and service module promoted from dead payload to a fourth stage so the flight plan can brake with the engine Apollo actually braked with. Translunar injection is 3162 m/s at T+15325 s; the insertion is five and a half minutes long and has to start two hundred seconds before closest approach, and 725 m/s of it leaves the vehicle in a 1926 by 1776 km lunar orbit.
mission.apollo-lunar.history: Apollo's own answer to arriving somewhere: the service module carried an engine of its own, 91 kN at 314 seconds, and it was that engine rather than the launcher that braked the stack into lunar orbit.
mission.apollo-mars.here: So the lunar module comes off, which takes the third stage's throw from 3668 to 4891 m/s and makes the transfer possible. 3690 m/s at T+4500 s buys a heliocentric aphelion of 1.62 AU; the same burn three thousand seconds earlier buys 1.07 AU, which is not a transfer at all. Arrival is at T+186 days and 2410 m/s of braking leaves a 95159 by 91139 km orbit. Five metres a second either way on the injection is a crater.
mission.apollo-mars.history: No Apollo hardware ever went to Mars, and the arithmetic says why: the stack that could throw a lunar module towards the Moon falls short of the shape a Mars transfer needs, however the launch window is chosen.
mission.apollo-return.here: One burn, aimed four days ahead, and the landscape around it is not gentle. 3192 m/s at T+15295 s passes 3226 km over the Moon and arrives home at T+8.27 days at 7.4 degrees below the horizontal, pulling 14 g. A metre a second less steepens that to 17 degrees and 100 g; seven less hits the Moon. There is no entry model behind the verdict — the g-load is on the graph to be read.
mission.apollo-return.history: A free return is a trajectory that comes home whether or not anything else works: round the far side of the Moon and back into the atmosphere, on the injection alone. It is the trajectory Apollo 13 was on when its service module failed.
mission.apollo-saturn.here: The only preset that can be checked against a flight that happened, so the numbers are worth keeping close: first staging at T+159 s against the real 161, insertion at T+604 s into 192 by 186 km, 8965 m/s spent and 45 m/s of it lost to drag against the real forty-odd. It ends at the parking orbit on purpose — the translunar burn is sitting in the tank.
mission.apollo-saturn.history: Saturn V, 2938 tonnes on the pad, five F-1 engines and 33.6 MN off it. Apollo 11 dropped the first stage at T+161 s and entered a 186 by 183 km parking orbit at T+699 s, with four fifths of the third stage's propellant still aboard for the burn towards the Moon.
mission.earth-falcon.here: The reference flight of this simulator, and the one whose figures are quoted everywhere else. It reaches 304 by 239 km for 8995 m/s, with max q of 43 kPa at 11 km and a peak of 5.9 g. That total is below the real 9.3 to 9.5 km/s for one reason: the pad here sits on the equator and is handed all 465 m/s of the planet's rotation.
mission.earth-falcon.history: Falcon 9 is the two-stage kerosene launcher that made reuse ordinary: nine Merlin 1D engines on the first stage, one vacuum Merlin on the second, and about 22 tonnes to low orbit when the booster comes home.
mission.io-jupiter.here: The only preset where the sphere of influence is a design constraint rather than bookkeeping: Io's is 7840 km, four and a third radii, so the parking orbit has to be 58 by 43 km. Leaving does not need escape — 417 m/s reaches the edge — but the preset spends 750, because that is the value whose Jupiter orbit does not wander back in. Which way out it goes depends on where in the parking orbit the burn happens: Io is going round Jupiter at 17 km/s.
mission.io-jupiter.history: Io is the innermost of the Galilean moons and the most volcanically active body in the solar system, held in a tidal grip by a planet three hundred times the mass of everything else put together.
mission.kerbin-ascent.here: The numbers are the game's, cliff and all — every other atmosphere here is cut off where its density reaches Earth's ceiling value, and Kerbin's is cut off where the game says so. A planet that small under air that thick does not yield to a single continuous burn, so the second stage is set to light at apoapsis. 122 by 92 km for 3772 m/s.
mission.kerbin-ascent.history: Kerbin is not real. It is the home planet of Kerbal Space Program: 600 km across with one g at the surface, wearing an Earth-thick atmosphere that ends abruptly at 70 km, which is a combination physics does not offer anywhere.
mission.kerbin-mun.here: The cheapest mission here to fly and the fiddliest to aim. 868 m/s away and 350 to stay, and the transfer is aimed *past* the Mun on purpose: with 364 m/s of hyperbolic excess against a body this small the grazing impact parameter is 486 km, so everything from 851 to 861 m/s ends in a crater and the miss has to be bought with another seven.
mission.kerbin-mun.history: The Mun is Kerbin's moon, and the first place most players of that game ever land — or, more often, arrive at rather faster than intended.
mission.mars-ascent.here: A light two-stage launcher to 249 by 195 km. It is the only pitch programme here whose tail goes *below* the horizon: eighteen degrees down at the end of the burn is what stops the climb while the horizontal speed is still building, and it is the only thing in that family that raises a periapsis rather than an apoapsis. Mars's air is modelled to 150 km, which is where its profile reaches the density Earth's own ceiling cuts off at.
mission.mars-ascent.history: Nothing has launched from Mars either. What would have to work there is thin air — six millibars — over a third of Earth's gravity, which is a much easier ascent than Titan's and a much harder arrival.
mission.moon-ascent.here: A vacuum ascent, and the cheapest flight in the collection: 1976 m/s to a 53 by 48 km orbit. With no air there is no maximum dynamic pressure to mark, no Mach number to report and no temperature the model is willing to invent — the environment panel reads zero because that is honest.
mission.moon-ascent.history: Six Apollo lunar modules lifted off from the Moon, into the only kind of ascent where drag does not exist and the whole budget goes into speed.
mission.parker-solar.here: The only mission here that spends its energy going *down*: the injection is aimed against the Earth's own motion, so what it buys is not distance but the loss of heliocentric angular momentum, and every Venus flyby takes more away. Three of them — at 46, 495 and 1169 days, each brought round by the resonance the one before it left — walk the perihelion from 39 solar radii to 23.7, where the vehicle is doing 119 km/s. The flybys are aims rather than numbers: each says which side of Venus to pass and how close, and the correction is solved for when the moment comes. Three is what 52 kg of hydrazine buys; the real mission's other four are bought with geometry, over years of design.
mission.parker-solar.history: The Parker Solar Probe launched in 2018 on the highest departure energy ever flown, and spent seven years and seven Venus flybys walking its perihelion down to 9.9 solar radii, where it passes at 190 km/s inside the corona.
mission.proton-geo.here: The preset that needed the most from the flight plan: three burns, a spent stage jettisoned mid-plan and five and a half hours of coasting between the second and the third. What is measured at the end is not the altitude but the period — 23.927 hours against the sidereal day's 23.934, which for a real satellite is a slow drift east and a station-keeping budget.
mission.proton-geo.history: Blok DM is the restartable upper stage that made Soviet geostationary launches possible: a burn to a transfer orbit, a long coast out to apogee, and another burn to circularise where the day is exactly as long as the satellite's year.
mission.proton-zvezda.here: Proton-K is here rather than a Soyuz because it is serial — three stages in a line — and a serial list cannot honestly hold four boosters burning alongside a core. The third stage is cut off with 3.3 tonnes left, and 43 m/s of that at the first apoapsis gives 513 by 408 km with the low side exactly at the station's altitude. Baikonur is at 51.6 degrees and this simulator has one plane, so the pad is handed 465 m/s it never had.
mission.proton-zvezda.history: Zvezda, the service module of the International Space Station, went up on a Proton-K in July 2000. The launcher put it in an ellipse a couple of hundred kilometres up and the module climbed to the station over the following days on its own engines.
mission.saved.here: Nothing here is a preset: whatever you left in the four columns is what this will fly. The figures beside are read straight out of it.
mission.saved.history: Your own setup, as you last saved it from the editor.
mission.titan-ascent.here: The hardest ascent here, and not for the reason it looks. The air is four times as dense as Earth's at the surface, sound travels at 199 m/s and terminal velocity at full thrust is 173 m/s — a rocket cannot go fast in it, so it cannot turn low. The answer is nine minutes of climbing straight up and a kick stage at apoapsis, which reaches 1212 by 1072 km with 619 m/s lost to drag.
mission.titan-ascent.history: Titan has a nitrogen atmosphere at one and a half bars over a surface where gravity is a seventh of Earth's. Nothing has ever launched from it; Huygens only came down through it, and measured the temperature profile this model uses.
mission.voyager-tour.here: Four gravity assists on one injection, and no thrust after it: Jupiter at T+1.7 years, Saturn at 4.3, Uranus at 12.0, Neptune at 22.7, and out past 34 AU by the thirtieth. Each pass grows the orbit — 23 AU of aphelion after Jupiter, 30 after Saturn, 58 after Uranus. The launcher is a Titan IIIE / Centaur, whose two solid boosters burn first and alone, which is what lets a serial stage list hold it honestly.
mission.voyager-tour.history: Voyager 2 left in 1977 and flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, the only spacecraft ever to visit the last two. It arrived at Neptune twelve years after launch, on an alignment that comes round once in about 175 years, and it is still going.

setup.argPeri.info: Which way the closest point of the orbit faces. On a circle it does nothing; on an ellipse it turns the whole ellipse about the parent.
setup.bodyDiameter.info:
The diameter of the rocket's body. The reference area A = πd²/4 follows from it, and drag is applied to that.

The relationship is quadratic: a rocket twice as wide catches four times the air. Shape is not modelled — everything that does not reduce to area is hidden in the drag coefficient.
setup.cd.info:
The drag coefficient. Drag is computed as ½·ρ·v²·Cd·A, so the relationship is linear.

The model knows nothing about the rocket's shape and does not vary Cd with Mach number: this is one averaged figure for the whole flight. For a slender launcher 0.3–0.5 is reasonable, though real vehicles climb well above that briefly around Mach 1.
setup.composition.info:
The mole fractions of the gases in the atmosphere. They are normalised automatically, so percentages or any other proportions will do.

Exactly two things come out of the mixture: the molar mass — a heavy gas hugs the surface and gives a small scale height — and the adiabatic index γ, which fixes the speed of sound. Nothing else depends on it: there is no chemistry in the model.
setup.cutoff.info:
How many seconds after ignition to shut the engine down rather than run the tanks dry. Zero means burn to the last drop.

This is the main instrument of a precise insertion: the orbit you end up in is decided by when the last stage stops. A few extra seconds of thrust raise the apoapsis by hundreds of kilometres.
setup.density.info:
The planet's mean density. The mass follows from it and the radius: M = ρ·(4/3)πR³.

Handy when you would rather say what the body is made of than pick a number: a rocky planet sits near 5500 kg/m³, an icy or gassy one at a third of that. Earth is 5514.
setup.diameter.info:
The planet's diameter. Together with the second independent figure — mass, density or surface gravity — it fixes everything else: the gravitational parameter μ = GM, the surface acceleration and the orbital speeds.

A large radius at the same density means both stronger gravity and a faster orbit: circular speed grows roughly as √(R·g). A small planet forgives almost any rocket; a large one forgives almost none.
setup.dryMass.info:
The mass of the stage without propellant: tanks, engines, structure. It has to be accelerated just like the payload, but it adds no propellant.

This is what limits a stage's Δv. Tsiolkovsky cares about the ratio of start mass to end mass, and the dry mass is the denominator you cannot get below.
setup.ecc.info:
How far from circular the orbit is. Zero is a circle; 0.9 is a long thin ellipse that spends most of its time far out and crosses the near part quickly.

The sphere of influence is computed from the semi-major axis alone, so a very eccentric moon will reach outside its own sphere near apoapsis. Nothing breaks, but the capture geometry stops making sense.
setup.ignitionDelay.info:
The pause between separation and lighting this stage, when the mode is set to a delay.

A short pause simply loses a little speed to gravity. A long one turns into a ballistic coast towards apoapsis — though the "at apoapsis" mode is easier for that, since it finds the moment itself.
setup.ispSL.info:
Specific impulse at the planet's surface pressure. Between this and the vacuum figure, Isp is interpolated linearly against ambient pressure.

This is where the thrust loss at liftoff comes from. An engine built for vacuum shows a wide gap; with no atmosphere the figure simply never matters.
setup.ispVac.info:
Specific impulse in vacuum, in seconds. It is really the exhaust velocity divided by g₀: 300 s means 2943 m/s.

The defining number of an engine. It alone fixes a stage's Δv for a given mass ratio, and together with thrust it sets the propellant flow. Kerosene and oxygen give around 310–350 s, hydrogen upwards of 450.
setup.mass.info:
The planet's mass. With the radius it gives the gravitational parameter μ = GM, which is all gravity knows about a planet. Surface acceleration, circular speed and escape speed all follow from it.

The density and gravity below are derived and update as you type. To define the planet through one of those instead, use the radio buttons above.
setup.meanAnom.info:
Where the body is at liftoff, measured along its orbit. This is the launch window: whether a transfer arrives at the moon or at the empty space it left is decided here.

Nothing in this simulator is tied to a date, so the shipped figures put the bodies where they make a picture worth looking at rather than where they were on any particular morning.
setup.noAir: This body has no atmosphere: a vacuum, and nothing to fly through.
setup.orbitAltitude.info:
The altitude you are aiming for. It steers nothing: the rocket is flown by the pitch programme alone.

It drives the dashed ring on the flight screen, the circular speed shown below, and the estimate of what is needed for orbit at the bottom. A target, not an autopilot.
setup.payload.info:
Payload is the mass of whatever the launch exists for: a satellite, a spacecraft, cargo. It rides all the way to orbit and is never dropped, so it counts towards the mass during every phase of the flight and in every stage of the rocket equation.

Adding to it costs more than it looks: lifting one more tonne needs propellant to accelerate that tonne, and then more propellant to accelerate that propellant. The Δv margin at the bottom of the screen falls noticeably faster than the mass rises.
setup.pitchHintAngles: 90° is straight up, 0° is the horizon.
setup.propellant.info:
The stage's working mass — fuel and oxidiser together. It is consumed at a constant rate while the engine runs.

The burn time is that mass divided by the flow, both shown below. Adding propellant pays off only up to a point: Δv grows logarithmically while the mass to lift grows linearly.
setup.readyHint: Ready to launch. Press Enter or the button on the right.
setup.rootNote: The root of the system: everything else goes round it.
setup.rotationPeriod.info:
How long the planet takes to turn once. The launch pad rides with it and hands the rocket 2πR/T for free — on Earth that is 465 m/s if you launch east from the equator.

The atmosphere turns with the planet too, so drag is computed against moving air rather than against the inertial frame. Zero means a planet that does not rotate.
setup.semiMajor.info:
The average distance from the parent body. It sets the orbital period on its own: T = 2π√(a³/μ), so a moon twice as far out takes 2.8 times as long to go round.

Gm is a million kilometres. The Moon sits at 0.384; the Earth at 149.6 from the Sun.
setup.sepDelay.info:
The pause between a stage shutting down and separating. For that whole time the spent stage is still attached and still has to be carried.

In reality the delay lets the thrust tail off and the mechanism clear. Here it is simply a few seconds of dead weight.
setup.stageLimit: Four stages is the limit here.
setup.surfaceGravity.info:
The gravitational acceleration at the surface. The mass follows from it and the radius: M = g·R²/G.

The most direct way to describe a planet: g says outright how hard it will be to leave the pad. The thrust-to-weight figure at the bottom of the screen is measured against it.
setup.surfacePressure.info:
The pressure at the surface. The whole barometric profile stands on it: the density at any altitude is proportional to it, and so is the drag.

It also sets the reference for specific impulse — the sea-level Isp applies at exactly this pressure, and Isp is interpolated linearly between it and vacuum. Zero means a planet with no atmosphere.
setup.temperature.info:
The temperature at the surface. It sets the scale height H = RT/(Mg): the warmer the gas, the more slowly it thins out with altitude.

It also fixes the speed of sound, and with it the Mach number and the whole transonic part of the climb. Higher up the temperature follows the lapse rates in the layer table.
setup.throttle.info:
The fraction of full thrust, 0 to 1. It stays constant for the whole burn.

The flow drops in proportion, so the propellant lasts longer while the total Δv is unchanged — only the rate of spending it. Throttling down keeps acceleration and dynamic pressure in check, at the price of a longer climb.
setup.thrustVac.info:
The engine's thrust in vacuum at full throttle. With the specific impulse it sets the mass flow: ṁ = F/(Isp·g₀).

At the surface the thrust is lower — ambient pressure pushes back on the nozzle exit. The model holds the flow constant and varies the thrust with altitude, following the specific impulse.
setup.timeLimit.info:
How much simulated time the flight is given. When it runs out the run stops with a time-limit verdict.

It exists for ballistic arcs that would otherwise take a very long time to come down, and for orbits where nothing further is going to happen.
setup.upperBoundary.info:
The altitude above which the model treats the air as absent. Density there is exactly zero, and so is drag.

It is also the success threshold: an orbit counts as achieved once the periapsis clears this mark. Put it where the density is already negligible, or a flight will be declared a success while the rocket is still in the air.
setup.warnDv: Total Δv falls short even before losses.
setup.warnTwr: Thrust-to-weight below 1 — the vehicle will not leave the pad.
